1:
Barnes explains the reckoning: the name means the fiftieth, counted from the sixteenth of Abib when the firstfruits were offered, whence the feast is also called the feast of weeks and of harvest. Gill insists the day was begun and not over, since it was the third hour when Peter preached, and that Pentecost was kept one day alone, two being observed only in the captivity for uncertainty of the calendar. Henry takes the phrase the same way, that the night preceding with part of the day was past, and traces the count to the firstfruits, offered on the day Christ arose. Robertson reports Blass for the view that Luke's present tense shows the day had not yet come and Hackett for the fifty-day interval, and observes that this Pentecost apparently fell on the Jewish Sabbath.

Why this day is answered in like terms by very different men. Henry gives three reasons: the concourse of people from all parts, which would spread the fame of it further; the feast's memorial of the law given on Sinai, which Lightfoot reckons at one thousand four hundred and forty-seven years earlier, so that the evangelical law is fitly promulgated in fire and tongues, not to one nation but to every creature; and its falling on the first day of the week, which he takes for a confirmation of the Christian sabbath as a memorial of the resurrection and the outpouring together. Leo counts from the other end, the tenth day from the Ascension and the fiftieth from the Resurrection, finding mysteries new and old by which it is manifest that Grace was fore-announced through the Law and the Law fulfilled through Grace. Calvin reports Augustine's version of the argument, that as the law was written on stone fifty days after the Passover so the Spirit, whose office is to write it on our hearts, came as many days after the resurrection of the true Passover; he will not refute it, objecting only that it is pressed as necessary. Wesley compresses it into a phrase, the Pentecost of Sinai and the Pentecost of Jerusalem, the legal manifestation and the evangelical, the one from the mountain and the other from heaven, the terrible and the merciful.

On the place and the company Ellicott observes that of all the feasts this drew the largest number of pilgrims from distant lands, the dangers of travel thinning the Passover and Tabernacles, so that no other season was so likely to produce immediate results. Barnes puts the same providence as delay, the Spirit being withheld until the greatest number of Jews should be gathered at Jerusalem, both to preach where the Lord was crucified and to send the gospel thence into distant parts. Henry adds that Jerusalem, which had done Christ the utmost dishonour imaginable, received this honour from him; Cyril of Jerusalem claims the day for his own city, speaking not of good things that happened among others but of those vouchsafed among ourselves. Lightfoot alone unsettles the date, questioning whether the Spirit was poured out on the very day of the Jewish Pentecost, since no fitter reason can be invented why they should be all with one accord in one place than a gathering to keep the Lord's day; he takes the all for the hundred and twenty, as does Wesley, who calls it a conjunction of company, minds and place.

Chrysostom looks past the calendar to the type. Pentecost was the season when the sickle was put to the harvest; now the time was come to put in the sickle of the word, and the Spirit came down keen-edged as that sickle, Christ having first taken the firstfruits and borne them on high. Clarke, whose note here is an analysis of the whole chapter, keeps to the plain sequence: the day arrived, the disciples assembled, and the Spirit descended as a mighty rushing wind.
2:
On the sound, philology divides them from physics. Ellicott and Robertson note that the word rendered wind is a cognate of the word for Spirit, so the phrase is better given as a mighty breath borne onwards, Ellicott connecting it with Peter's men of old borne on by the Holy Ghost, Robertson observing that it was no wind at all but a roar as of a mighty wind rushing. Clarke takes it physically, that thunder is meant, the harbinger of the divine presence, and explains the rushing by a great passage of electrical fluid and the air pouring into the vacuum behind it, comparing the wind and fire that prepared Elijah for the still small voice. Gill hears in the suddenness the freeness of the gift, unasked and undeserved, and a symbol of the gospel going into all the earth. Cyril of Jerusalem calls it a heavenly trumpet and makes the house the vessel of spiritual water, so that those within were entirely baptized; Wesley notes only that so will the Son of man come to judgment.

Calvin gives the fullest account of why signs were needed: our slothfulness is such that unless God wakes every sense his power passes unknown, and the signs were given less for the disciples than for us. The violence of the wind was to make them afraid, since we are never rightly prepared for grace until the confidence of the flesh is tamed; and wind commonly signifies the Spirit, the very word being borrowed from breath because that person of the divine essence is in itself incomprehensible.

The fiery tongues are read two ways. Clarke has the flashes frequent at first and then a lambent flame settling stationary on each head, proof that the Spirit had made each man his temple, and gathers parallels from Sinai, from rabbinic pictures of teachers ringed with fire, and from a Persian painting of Abraham crowned with flame. Ellicott denies that the word can mean cloven, since it always signifies dividing, and describes a shower of fiery tongues coming they knew not whence, lighting a moment on each head and vanishing, the verb for sitting being in the tense of momentary action. Robertson takes the participle as middle, the appearance presenting itself first as one body and then parting, and insists the point is not that each tongue was cloven but that each looked like fire without being fire. Barnes notes that the phrase tongue of fire occurs once only in the Old Testament, and that tongue is used of whatever resembles it. Gill makes the tongues an emblem of the languages, and this the baptism with fire John foretold; Wesley allows they were small flames only, yet thinks they may intimate God touching their tongues with divine fire; Lightfoot reads the shape against the confusion of languages at Babel.

Whether the miracle lay in mouth or ear is the sharpest question. Calvin reports the opinion that they spoke one tongue only and the same sound was diversely distributed among the hearers, a conjecture resting on Peter afterwards preaching one sermon to many nations. Wesley rejects it as unaccountably supposed, placing the wonder in the mouth of the speakers, and adds that this family praising God in the tongues of all the world was an earnest that the whole world should praise him in its own. Barnes and Robertson agree, the one that no natural account of the thing will serve, the other that each spoke a real language he had never learned, not jargon, and that Paul's rule requiring an interpreter disposes of the modern imitations. Ellicott reads the passage through the Corinthian chapter, where the tongue edifies none but the speaker, and insists from the context that the gift was not confined to the apostles, the women sharing it; Gill extends it past the twelve to the seventy and perhaps all the hundred and twenty.
5:
The word for dwelling is weighed first. Robertson and Ellicott agree that it means settled residence rather than a pilgrim's sojourning, though Ellicott allows it wide enough for worshippers come up to the feast, and Barnes suggests that wealthy foreign Jews kept houses at Jerusalem to be near the temple, the more likely because the Messiah was then expected. Clarke divides the devout men into Jews born abroad and proselytes, both come up for the feast and for trade, there being scarcely a commercial nation where Jews had not settled. Henry divides them into proselytes of righteousness who were circumcised and proselytes of the gate who forsook idolatry without the ceremonial law, calls every nation under heaven hyperbolical, and adds that Jerusalem was then the rendezvous of religious people as Tyre once was of trading ones. Gill has them come to learn Hebrew or to increase in piety, and Calvin sees God gathering in every age some remaining seed into that city while the temple still served some use.

What drew the crowd is sharply answered. Ellicott insists the noun is never used in the New Testament for rumour but always of an utterance, so the sense is when there had been this voice; Robertson notes it is not the word used of the rushing sound and takes the tongues themselves to have been loud enough to gather the city. Clarke, holding to his thunder, has the city alarmed and flocking to the temple. Calvin adds why it mattered: had men heard the apostles at different places and times the miracle would have been far less famous, so they are brought into one place that the diversity of tongues may appear by comparison.

The wonder turns on who the speakers were. Barnes recalls that Galileans were proverbially ignorant and their dialect corrupt, the name a reproach, so their ignorance made the miracle the more striking; Robertson adds that they were not strong on language and yet are the very people who show such linguistic powers. Calvin names two causes of wonder, that private and unlearned men born in a base corner should treat profoundly of heavenly matters, and that new tongues were given them suddenly. Ellicott observes that this answers to what Paul says of the gift, a sign to unbelievers while the converting work is left to prophecy. Clarke grants that some suppose the miracle wrought on the hearers rather than the speakers, but holds it the same either way, as much power being needed to make an Arab understand a Galilean as to make a Galilean speak Arabic.

Of the list Barnes notes that it begins at the east and runs westward, Henry that it starts with the posterity of Shem and names Judea because, though the language was the same there, the Galileans spoke it with a north-country tone. Ellicott renders the Romans as sojourners and prefers the majesty of God to the wonderful works, the phrase pointing to praise and not teaching; Robertson reports Knowling for the Cretes and Arabians being an afterthought, and insists the point is not that each group had its own language but that wherever a local tongue existed it was heard spoken. Wesley takes the one island for all. On the mockery he and Gill assign it to the natives of Jerusalem, who understood none of these tongues, Wesley tracing the world's progress from mocking to cavilling, threats, imprisonment, blows and at last slaughter; Lightfoot matches the taunt to a rabbinic idiom in which men made mellow at Purim were said to be sweetened, and Calvin calls it monstrous to scoff at what could scarcely be plainer if God descended visibly. Cyril of Jerusalem turns the jeer round: they spoke truly though in mockery, for the wine was new indeed, the grace of the New Testament from a spiritual Vine that had borne fruit in the prophets and now budded anew.
14:
Henry sets the sermon in its place. It was preached not to the strangers in their own languages but to the Jews in the vulgar tongue, and to the mockers in particular, the other disciples meanwhile speaking the wonderful works of God to those who understood them; and three thousand were converted by the preaching of most of the hundred and twenty, only Peter's sermon being recorded as evidence that he who had denied his Lord so meanly now confessed him so courageously. He adds that the men of greatest authority confronted those who contradicted while the seventy were left to the willing proselytes, so that among Christ's ministers some of greater gifts take hold of sword and spear and others are vine-dressers. Ellicott marks the change in the man, timidity become boldness and a few hasty words become elaborate discourse, with a method in handling prophecy unlike anything seen in him before, so that a writer of fiction would be blamed for the inconsistency. Gill has the eleven rise at once as abhorring the charge, Peter standing in their midst as their mouth; Robertson notes that Luke alone uses the phrase for lifting up the voice; Calvin observes that they rose because men rise when they wish to be better heard.

Clarke corrects the address, that those dwelling at Jerusalem were not inhabitants of Judea but the sojourners already listed, while Wesley takes the men of Judea for those born there, notes that Peter spoke in Hebrew, and divides the discourse into three parts, each opening with the same appellation and the last adding the more familiar word brethren. Chrysostom observes that it was divinely ordered that some should mock, since the jeer gave Peter a starting-point for his defence and by that defence he could teach. Barnes finds the boldness characteristic of the man and draws the rule that no ridicule should deter Christians from an honest avowal.

The answer to the charge rests on the hour. Barnes reckons the third hour at nine in the morning and gives the reasons why drunkenness was then improbable, chief among them that it was the hour of morning worship. Clarke says the Jews scarcely ate or drank before that hour, the custom being so settled that even the intemperate did not transgress it, and Wesley that on the solemn festivals they rarely ate or drank till noon. Ellicott appeals to common feeling, that drunkenness belonged to the night and rising early to follow strong drink was a mark of extremest baseness, asking whether these men were likely to be drunk at nine after a night in devotion when all decent Jews were fasting. Robertson calls it a quick, common-sense reply; Calvin makes it a probable argument, that men are not commonly drunk betimes in the morning; Gill notes that the denial covers the whole hundred and twenty on whom the Spirit was poured. Cyril of Jerusalem turns the hour into another kind of argument: he who was crucified at the third hour now at the third hour sent down his grace, the grace of the Spirit being not other than his own, so that he who gave the promise made it good.

The appeal to Joel follows. Gill notes that the Jews themselves allow the prophecy to belong to the world to come, which in their usage means the times of the Messiah; Barnes observes that the citation follows neither the Hebrew nor the Greek exactly though it keeps the substance; Clarke takes the fulfilment as further proof that the Jesus they crucified is the Messiah; and Robertson marks the moment as the first interpretation of the life and work of Christ since the Ascension, Peter's mind being now opened to see prophecy and fulfilment together. Wesley puts it most simply, that there is another and better way of accounting for this.
17:
Peter's first alteration of the prophet is noticed by all. Where Joel has afterwards he puts in the last days, and Gill cites Kimchi that the two mean the same, the days of the Messiah being intended wherever the last days are named; Clarke says the phrase was so understood among the Jews, Wesley that the times of the Messiah are frequently so called, Robertson that Joel defines those days rather as the day of the Lord. Calvin defends the change as exposition rather than addition, since a prophecy of the perfect restoring of the Church can belong to no age but the last, while Barnes traces the expression through the Old Testament as meaning simply future times.

On the breadth of the promise they are pointed. Wesley takes all flesh for persons of every age, sex and rank, and explains the visions given to the young and dreams to the old by the vigour of the outward senses in the one and the inward in the other. Clarke reports Rabbi Tanchum, that in the old text each prophet prophesied singly but in the times of the Messiah all Israel shall be prophets, and observes that since the Jews held the spirit of prophecy never rested on a poor man, the naming of menservants and maidservants shows that neither bond nor free nor male nor female is shut out. Ellicott calls this the culminating point of the prediction, the gift falling not on priests but on slaves. Barnes notes that where the Hebrew has the servants both the Greek and Peter read my servants, so the sense is the servants of God rather than a rank of society, and Calvin presses the same restriction, that God does not profane his Spirit by making it common to despisers.

The terrors are read very differently. Clarke refers the wonders and the darkened sun to the calamities that fell on the Jews at the destruction of Jerusalem, the blood and fire and smoke being skirmishes and the wasting of the country; Gill supplies a particular, the comet that hung over Jerusalem like a flaming sword. Barnes treats the images as emblems, the sun's shining standing for prosperity and its withdrawing for calamity. Ellicott draws the imagery from a Palestinian thunderstorm, the lurid blood-red sky and columns of cloud, and suspects that Peter, not yet knowing the times and seasons, looked for the great day within his own lifetime. Robertson makes the sharpest observation, that Peter treats the portents as already fulfilled although no darkening of the sun is recorded, so that he plainly does not read Joel's symbolism in literal terms. Wesley spreads the fulfilment across four occasions, the signs before the passion, at the passion and resurrection, at the destruction of Jerusalem and at the end of the world; Calvin refuses both narrower readings and takes the day for the whole kingdom of Christ from the first preaching. Cyril of Jerusalem keeps to the end, the Lord coming from heaven with glory in the last day, this created world passing away that a fairer may be made manifest.

The promise at the close is what Peter was after. Ellicott notes that the phrase to call upon God, common in the Old Testament, never occurs in the Gospels but is a favourite with Luke and Paul, its Greek associations giving it almost the force of an appeal to a higher tribunal. Robertson takes the middle voice as calling for oneself in need, and Wesley finds in the words the whole of religion and particularly prayer in faith. Calvin calls it an excellent place: God pricks us forward like sluggish asses with threats, and having brought darkness on heaven and earth still shows a means by which salvation may shine before our eyes; a simple promise would be much, but it is far more to promise it amidst so many dungeons of death.
22:
Chrysostom watches the tactics. The title men of Israel is not flattery but relief, Peter having borne hard on them and reminding them now of their great ancestor; he begins afresh with an introduction so that they may not be stirred, for while the prophet was the subject there was nothing to excite them, but the name of Jesus would. Ellicott feels the boldness from the other side, barely seven weeks having passed since the bearer of that name died the death of a slave, and the speaker had denied all knowledge of him. Barnes marks this the third part of the argument, to prove the resurrection and bring them to repent of putting their own Messiah to death; Gill notes that the Arabic version prefaces the words as though a new oration began, though the discourse is continuous. Clarke glosses approved as celebrated or famous, made known by miracles in such profusion as their best prophets never wrought; Ellicott takes the word in its older sense of proved or pointed out, and Robertson observes that Peter calls the audience itself to witness. Calvin says he comes to his point by little and little, the right use of every gift we have by Christ being to bring us to Christ as to a fountain; Cyril of Jerusalem gathers the prophetic testimonies to the Spirit from Micah and Haggai.

On the delivering up they divide over the agent. Gill spreads it across all of them, Christ delivering himself, the Father not sparing him, Judas selling him, the Jews handing him to Pilate. Robertson takes the verbal adjective, found nowhere else in the New Testament, to mean delivered up by Judas, while noting that purpose and foreknowledge stand in the same clause. Clarke reports two alternatives, Pearce's paraphrase that the word means given forth or sent into the world, and Kypke's contention that it refers not to God but to Judas; Barnes keeps the ordinary sense, of one surrendered to enemies by those who should have protected him. Ellicott finds a mark of genuineness in the vocabulary, the adjective recurring in Peter's later speech and the noun for foreknowledge in his epistle and nowhere else, and notes that it is now the habit of his mind to trace a divine purpose men cannot thwart. Henry states the two sides plainly: as God's act the death was of wonderful grace and wisdom, justice satisfied and God and man brought together by an eternal counsel that could not be altered; as the people's act it was awful sin and folly. Wesley meets the objection: God knew what those wicked men intended and could have blasted their designs in a moment, but did not exert that power because he so loved the world. Calvin adds why the death is mentioned at all, that the resurrection may be the more believed, the crucifixion being notorious and the rising a great token of divine power.

The loosing of the pains divides them again. Clarke reports the common view that the bonds detaining the dead were dissolved, Barnes sets the word against binding, and Ellicott and Wesley press the literal sense of travail-pangs, the word rendered sorrows elsewhere. Calvin takes the phrase deeper than bodily feeling: men who consider that death is the curse of God must conceive him angry in it, whence comes a horror worse than death itself, which Christ underwent in taking our guilt upon him. Wesley adds that it was not possible he should be held because the Scripture must be fulfilled. Ellicott and Robertson weigh the occasion: rumours had been met by the counter-story of the stolen body, and this was the first public witness, borne by a man ready to seal it with his blood; Robertson cites Furneaux, that at a time when the statement could still be tested the apostle proclaimed it as needing no evidence, being known to his hearers.
25:
Who speaks in the psalm is settled first. Clarke calls it a prophecy of which every word applies to Christ exclusively, and Gill says the whole psalm belongs to the Messiah. Ellicott is more careful, rendering the phrase in reference to him, and observing that read otherwise the psalm speaks only of the writer's own confidence, which some confine to a temporal deliverance and others extend to immortality. Robertson holds that there is but one speaker and that Peter, like Paul afterwards, makes him the Messiah, David giving his own experience as typical. Calvin explains why so much proof was needed: the resurrection had to be pressed on the Jews as a new thing, which is no marvel when the disciples themselves had profited so little from Christ's repeated teaching. Cyril of Jerusalem reads the psalm through as a whole, adding the line about the assemblies of blood he will not join, applying it to those who refused their king and chose Caesar.

The gladness is next. Barnes grounds the exultation in the Messiah's being preserved amid the sorrows coming on him, as one who for the joy set before him endured the cross. Calvin makes the sequence general: joy of soul, gladness of tongue and quietness of the whole body follow upon sure hope, since men not past feeling must be sorrowful while they feel themselves destitute of God's help. On the word rendered tongue Clarke observes that the Hebrew has my glory, which he takes for the soul; Ellicott says the term was applied to the mind of man as that in which he excelled all creatures, and that Peter follows the Greek paraphrase. Robertson notes that the flesh is said to tabernacle, to pitch its tent, in hope.

The hardest clause is the leaving in Hades. Clarke insists the word means the state of separate spirits, a general term among the Greeks covering Tartarus for the wicked and Elysium for the good. Robertson calls Hades the unseen world, here death itself considered as a rapacious destroyer, and denies that it means the place of punishment, since both heaven and torment lie within it and the terms are strictly parallel. Wesley is the most emphatic, that it does not appear our Lord ever went into hell, his soul passing at its separation to paradise, the meaning being only that God would not leave it in the separate state nor suffer the body to be corrupted. Ellicott reads it the other way, taking Peter's own later words about the spirits in prison to give the sense embodied afterwards in the article of the descent into hell. Calvin observes that two Hebrew words for the grave stand here, one so named because death is insatiable, whence the sayings that hell has enlarged her soul and that they open their mouth like the grave.

The last clause is read as the resurrection itself. Gill takes it that God made the risen Christ know experimentally the way from death to life, shown first to him as firstfruits. Barnes gives the idiom, the ways of life meaning the road to life as we speak of the road to honour, so the sense is thou wilt restore me to life; Clarke that it is the way back from the region of the dead, the same body resumed and the same life lived as before; Robertson that though dead he will be shown the ways back; Wesley that the filling with joy belongs to the ascension to God's right hand. Calvin holds that in Christ this was fulfilled without anything lacking, whereas the members have it by measure, so that he was far from corruption in order to be the firstfruits of them that rise. Ellicott declines to interpret the words, though he thinks Peter would have seen them fulfilled in Christ's humanity, filled with gladness even in Hades, being in the paradise of God.
29:
The argument turns on the tomb still standing. Ellicott renders the opening as it is lawful for me to speak with freedom, no hearer being able to pretend the psalm had been literally fulfilled in David, so that a fulfilment had to be looked for elsewhere. Robertson glosses the adverb as telling it all, with fulness and boldness. Gill notes that Peter now calls them brethren, having styled them only men of Judea before; Barnes remarks that he opens respectfully though they had just charged him with drunkenness, and draws the rule that Christians should keep the usual courtesies whatever contempt they meet. Clarke supplies a rabbinic saying, that neither worm nor insect had power over David, and thinks that if such an opinion was current Peter's appeal to the sepulchre was the sharper.

That David spoke of another is established two ways. Calvin gives both reasons: he was a prophet, and things removed from the knowledge of men are revealed to prophets, so it were wickedness to measure their speech by common capacity; and he had God's oath about his seed. Barnes adds that his being dead and buried made the words impossible of himself. Wesley presses the logic of the oath, that a kingdom promised and never received before death implies a resurrection, the kingdom being everlasting. Clarke and Ellicott turn textual critic here, Clarke reporting that the clause about raising up Christ according to the flesh is wanting in several manuscripts, rejected by Griesbach and pronounced by Professor White most certainly to be deleted, and Ellicott that without those words the sentence still runs, that God had sworn one of his loins should sit on his throne. Ellicott adds that what was untrue of the historical David was found true of the Christ.

From prophecy Peter passes to testimony. Barnes notes that if the rising were prophesied the only question left was whether it had happened; Ellicott observes that from the first the apostles take up the position their Lord assigned them, witnesses above all else of the resurrection; Calvin insists the text will bear no other sense than that they saw the risen Christ with their eyes, and Clarke has the whole hundred and twenty for witnesses.

On the exaltation the grammar is genuinely open. Robertson lays out three possible cases for the phrase about the right hand, instrumental, locative and dative, all of one form and all making sense. Barnes and Calvin take it instrumentally, the right hand standing everywhere in Scripture for power, so Christ was borne to heaven by God's might; Wesley says the same in a line. Ellicott prefers the instrument too, though the image beneath the phrase is of the Eternal King stretching out his hand to raise to a place beside him one who was in form his servant; Gill has the human nature raised to an honour never conferred on any creature. On the psalm that follows Gill observes that David's body was still in its sepulchre though his spirit had returned to God, Clarke that conquerors set their feet on the necks of the vanquished, Robertson that this dominion lasts until the plan of the kingdom is carried out. Wesley finds the quotation chosen with great address, warning the hearers in the words of their own prophetic monarch how certain their ruin must be if they oppose Christ; Cyril of Jerusalem gathers the other testimonies to the Son's sitting at the right hand, from the Gospel and from Peter's own epistle. The conclusion is plain: Calvin observes that Israel confessed a Christ was to come without knowing who, so the Jesus they handled so spitefully is the one they must acknowledge Lord; Ellicott notes the force of the order, that both Lord and Christ God made him; Clarke sums the discourse as proving the resurrection, the ascension, and the supreme government of Jews and Gentiles, angels and men.
37:
The wound the sermon made is examined closely. Robertson and Ellicott agree that the verb is rare and occurs here only in the New Testament, Robertson noting that Homer used it of horses denting the earth with their hoofs, Ellicott that it expresses the emotion we call compunction and that a noun from the same root is rendered slumber elsewhere, perhaps for the unconsciousness that follows extreme pain. Barnes insists there was no fanaticism in the discourse but cool, close, pungent reasoning, and that this prepared the effect. Clarke says the argument, supported everywhere by prophecy and matching fact, left them without reply and without excuse, so that they saw no hope but in the mercy of him they had crucified. Henry sets the whole scene in its place, that Peter never in his life spoke with such fulness and power, and that here we see the first-fruits of a vast harvest gathered in by a word mighty through God. Chrysostom draws a different lesson from the manner: gentleness pricks the heart more than any vehemence, for as with bodies grown callous the blow does not tell until they are first made tender, so here the hearers had first to be softened. Wesley catches the smallest sign of the change, that they now call the apostles brethren, which they had not done before, and Calvin marks the double fruit Luke records, that they were touched with sorrow and that they obeyed the counsel given them, which is the very beginning of repentance.

The answer is a command in two parts, and the commentators weigh each. Clarke renders repentance as humbling themselves before God, deploring the sins committed, praying earnestly for mercy and deprecating the displeasure of incensed justice; Barnes defines it as sorrow for sin as committed against God with a purpose to forsake it, and not merely a fear of the consequences or of wrath to come; Robertson puts it shortest, change your mind and your life, turn right about and do it now. Ellicott sets the apostolic work against the Baptist's as at once a continuation and a development, the same indispensable condition of repentance and the same outward symbol of purification and the same promise of forgiveness, but a baptism now in the name of Jesus Christ. Robertson marks the change of number and person in the Greek, that the plural command to repent is followed by a singular, let each one of you be baptized. Lightfoot takes up Beza's claim that the phrase declares not the form of baptism but its scope and end, and that the clause is wanting in the Syriac, answering that whatever copy Beza used the other copies have it.

What the promised gift is divides them. Wesley denies that it means the power of speaking with tongues, since the promise is made to all that are afar off in distant ages and nations, and takes it rather for the constant fruit of faith; Calvin makes the whole exchange an instance that none who ask at the mouth of the Lord go away empty, since the promise stands that to him who knocks it shall be opened, so that God will not suffer a godly desire to learn to be in vain. Gill notes only that Peter, as the mouth of the apostles, was ready with a word of comfort for distressed minds. Cyril of Jerusalem takes the two commands as answering the two parts of man: since man is soul and body the purification is twofold, the water cleansing the body and the Spirit sealing the soul, so that we draw near with the heart sprinkled and the body washed; and he bids the hearer make ready the vessel of his soul to become a son and an heir of God, putting off the old man of set purpose, for whatever he has done shall be forgiven him.
39:
How far the promise reaches is the question of the first verse. Robertson says the horizon widens here to include the Gentiles, since those afar off from the Jews were the heathen in the prophets and in the rabbis alike. Clarke agrees, taking it of the dispersed Jews and of all the Gentile nations, though he grants that Peter did not yet see how far his own words went. Ellicott makes the phrase wide enough to cover both, and observes that the tendency of sects has always been to claim spiritual gifts as the exclusive privilege of a few, whereas the essence of the appeal is that everyone Peter addresses may claim the promise as fully as he does. Gill lists what the promise may mean, the Messiah and salvation by him, or the remission of sins as a branch of the covenant, or the pouring out of the Spirit, and restricts the descendants to as many as belong to the election. Barnes takes it strictly of the influences of the Spirit, the very promise adduced at the opening of the discourse and now applied. Calvin explains why the clause had to be added, so that the Jews might persuade themselves the grace of Christ belonged to them as much as to the apostles, and insists that we cannot know the will of God except by his word.

Luke's own report is then admitted to be partial. Barnes calls this discourse, though one of the longest in the New Testament, no more than an outline, containing the substance of the plan of mercy. Robertson presses the two Greek words, that they mean not different words but further ones and more than these given, so that Luke does not pretend to report the whole. Ellicott suggests that the report breaks off as though the informant had followed closely to this point and then lost the sequence, and renders the verbs as continuing to testify and, in the passive, be ye saved. Gill says the same of the whole book, that Luke gives a compendium and not the sermons at length, the testimony being of Christ and against sins and errors. Calvin notes that Peter did not use doctrine only but added the pricks of exhortation and stood much upon it. Clarke reads the last charge as separation, that they should part from that generation and so be delivered from its unbelief and from the punishment awaiting it when the Romans destroyed the city; Ellicott and Wesley keep it a passive, an invitation to submit to God's way of salvation, Wesley adding that in such an accepted time we should add line upon line and not leave off till the thing is done, many of the generation being probably mocking still.

The harvest closes the section. Barnes and Clarke both dwell on the adverb, which means freely, cheerfully and willingly, Barnes taking it to imply that religion is not compulsion and that men become Christians without constraint, Clarke that they approved the doctrine, were glad to hear of this way of salvation, and began at once to act on it. Calvin makes the same word the definition of faith, that it must begin with this readiness and willing desire to obey. Gill supplies what they received, the doctrine of repentance and baptism and remission and the promise of the Spirit. Ellicott weighs the number against the mode, reporting the argument that three thousand makes affusion more likely than immersion and the considerations urged on the other side. Robertson observes that only those who accepted the word were baptized. Lightfoot sets the three thousand of this day beside the five thousand of the next chapter and refers both to the psalm, that the people shall be willing in the day of his power, the day of Christ's power being the day of his resurrection when he had subdued death and hell.
42:
Henry calls these verses the history of the truly primitive church in its infancy and its greatest innocence, and reads the first clause as diligence under preaching, since those discipled by baptism were discipled to be taught. Ellicott counts four elements of the new society's life here; Wesley numbers the same four as its daily communion, hearing the word, having all things common, receiving the Lord's Supper and prayer, and challenges the sects that all cry here is Christ to show him where the Christians live. Barnes marks the record as inspired testimony that they persevered, no apostasy being recorded though they were suddenly converted and much exposed to persecution. Robertson glosses fellowship from the word for a partner and what is common to all; Clarke takes it for association in religious things and denies that the community of goods can be meant, since that is mentioned two verses later. Calvin says Luke commends not the constancy of faith only but the exercises that confirm it, continual profiting under the apostles, much prayer, much fellowship and breaking of bread. Lightfoot explains the last phrase from Jewish custom, dinner beginning with blessing and breaking of bread, and Cyril of Jerusalem keeps the three thousand in view, caught in the spiritual net of Peter's words and continuing steadfastly in the apostles' doctrine and in the prayers.

The fear that followed is given a use. Gill spreads it over the inhabitants of Jerusalem, who had seen thousands profess a name that a few weeks before was in the utmost contempt. Barnes contrasts it with the derision of the morning, the power of God being so manifest that it silenced all clamour, which he takes for the ordinary effect of a great work of grace. Clarke reports manuscripts that read great fear and trembling upon every soul in Jerusalem, tracing it to weeks of astonishing miracles and preachers who charged the hearers home with a deliberate murder. Ellicott finds a distinction of tenses, the awe coming at that season while the signs were wrought continually, and Robertson makes both imperfects run together, so the more wonders the more fear. Calvin turns it to providence: the sight of the church frightened those who did not consent to its doctrine, and so preserved it, since novelty is odious and the Jews would not otherwise have suffered it to stand a day. Wesley says the same in a line, that the fear fell on those who did not join and so prevented persecution until it was needed.

On the community of goods they are careful to say what it was not. Robertson denies that it was actual communism, holding that they kept their property ready for the common good as need arose, and notes that the arrangement appears nowhere else. Ellicott says they had all things in common not by a compulsory abolition of property, and dwells with delight on what seemed to him the true ideal of a human society, founded not on self-interest and competition but on sympathy and self-denial; he notes too that the verbs throughout stand in the imperfect and so express a constantly recurring act, as Robertson also observes. Barnes reads the selling as of so much as was needed, distinguishing fixed property from movable. Calvin prefers to take the phrase rendered together of their agreement rather than a common dwelling, as when Luke says afterwards that they had one heart; Gill reads it the same way, no house being able to hold so many. Clarke sets out three possible senses of the phrase, in one time, in one place, or in one thing. Wesley answers the objection that the practice lasted only until Jerusalem fell, since many did it long after and no command required it, love constraining them; Lightfoot adds that houses and beds in Jerusalem were never let for hire.
46:
Why the disciples kept to the temple is answered several ways. Barnes says simply that this was the public place of worship and they were not disposed to leave where their fathers had worshipped, being there not constantly but at the customary hours of nine and three. Robertson observes that no breach had yet come between Christians and Jews. Ellicott feels the difficulty more sharply, that followers of a teacher whom the priests had condemned, and who had himself been nearly stoned and all but seized in those very courts, might have been expected to keep aloof from a sanctuary so desecrated, and answers from their memory that he had claimed it as his Father's house and that zeal for it had consumed him. Calvin gives a colder reason: they went not because drawn by any holiness of the place, since they knew the shadows of the law had ceased, nor to teach others to reverence it, but because the concourse of people there gave the best opportunity of furthering the gospel. Gill notes that they went up every day at the time of prayer, and Clarke that they were present at all the times of public worship, joining in prayer and praise, though it is not to be supposed they went on offering the sacrifices the law prescribed.

The breaking of bread is disputed again. Wesley takes it of the Lord's Supper, as many churches continued to do for some ages. Clarke offers a domestic reading, that companies living near one another ate together at their lodgings on returning from worship, and Robertson agrees that the phrase looks like the regular meal at home, leaving open whether a love-feast or the Supper followed. Barnes reports that the margin, with the Syriac and Arabic, renders the phrase at home rather than from house to house. Wesley draws the practical point from the same verse, that they carried one happy and holy temper through all their common actions, eating and working in the spirit in which they prayed.

The favour they enjoyed is qualified as carefully as it is reported. Barnes explains that it does not mean the people had become reconciled to Christianity, but that lives humble and devoted won the good will of the mass and silenced cavil, evidence that God can quiet opposition. Calvin says the same from the other side, that they were doubtless hated by many and that Luke speaks only of the sound part of the people, not yet infected with the poison of hatred, the favour being the ordinary fruit of an innocent life. Clarke observes that any upright Jew would esteem them for the simplicity and charity of their lives, the scandal of the cross not having yet begun. Ellicott traces the good will in part to their liberal almsgiving, and thinks the Sadducean priests the only section that watched them with malignant fear. Gill lists what they praised God for, temporal mercies and spiritual alike, that he had called them and revealed Christ and pardoned such sinners.

The last clause carries a textual question. Ellicott reports that many of the better manuscripts omit the words to the church and join the word rendered together with the opening of the next chapter; Robertson agrees that the phrase is not genuine, that the literal sense is simply together, and that Codex Bezae reads in the church. He notes that the verb is an imperfect, the Lord kept on adding, the same word used of the three thousand, and lets the wish escape him that the Lord always added those who join our churches.
